subject: St Macrina the Younger
sources_folder: design/saints-hub/sources/people/macrina-the-younger/ (gitignored; every quoted text saved there as .txt; check.py re-runs the word-for-word test)

life.text: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of St Macrina, translated by W. K. Lowther Clarke (SPCK, London, 1916), as transcribed by Roger Pearse on tertullian.org. Every quotation from the Life below was checked word for word against that transcription (case-insensitive, page marks and footnote numbers removed), and the key lines were also found in the archive.org scan of the printed 1916 book.
life.source: tertullian.org transcription; archive.org scan ldpd_11899093_000 (Columbia University Libraries copy)
life.note: LICENCE: published 1916, so public domain in the US; Roger Pearse's page says 'All material on this page is in the public domain - copy freely.' Clarke died in 1968, so in the UK the translation stays in copyright until 2038. The site already quotes Clarke (the 'tell' line). Clarke does NOT number chapters ('No attempt has been made to break up the matter into numbered sections', his introduction), so the Life is cited here by his section headings (e.g. 'the part headed Her betrothal') plus the Migne column (PG 46) he prints, for the checker. Readers should see only 'Life of Macrina' and the part in words, never the column numbers. Scan: https://archive.org/details/ldpd_11899093_000

dialogue.text: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection, translated by William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF second series vol. 5 (1893). Checked against CCEL's plain-text volume (marked Public Domain) and New Advent's copy of the same translation.
dialogue.source: CCEL npnf205 (whole dialogue on one page) and New Advent 2915
dialogue.note: The two copies differ in small ways. CCEL prints 'the especial pain' where New Advent has 'the special pain'; CCEL prints "all" and "in all" in quotation marks in the 1 Corinthians 15:28 passage and "grieved for them that sleep" / "men without hope" in the opening, where New Advent drops the marks. Prefer CCEL's wording (the 1893 print, unrevised). The dialogue has no chapters in NPNF; places are given by topic and by how far into the dialogue they fall.

born.text: About 330. Probably at or near Neocaesarea in Pontus, today Niksar in Turkey. Some put her birth at Caesarea in Cappadocia, today Kayseri.
born.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), 'St. Macrina the Younger': 'Born about 330; died 379.' New Catholic Encyclopedia, 2nd ed., 'Macrina, Ss.' (D. Meehan): 'b. Neocaesarea, Cappadocia, c. 330'. Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Neocaesarea': 'now called Niksar'. OCA: 'born in Cappadocia at the beginning of the fourth century'.
born.note: Dates differ. The site's 'c. 327' has only a weak source (Women in World History, via encyclopedia.com, which also calls her a 'Byzantine composer, singer', so it is not reliable); Wikidata lists 324, 327 and 330. The Episcopal Church's Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 says '340-379'. Plain wording that holds: 'About 330'. Neocaesarea was in Pontus (NCE's 'Neocaesarea, Cappadocia' is loose). The Life itself does not say where she was born. Kayseri for Caesarea: Women in World History only; not needed on the page.

grew_up.text: On the family's estates in Pontus. Her mother taught her at home, from the Bible rather than the poets: the Wisdom of Solomon and the Psalms. She said the Psalms at every part of the day.
grew_up.source: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'Macrina's childhood': 'such parts of inspired Scripture as you would think were incomprehensible to young children were the subject of the girl's studies; in particular the Wisdom of Solomon'; 'the Psalter was her constant companion, like a good fellow-traveller that never deserted her.'
grew_up.note: Clarke's introduction: the family 'had estates in Cappadocia and Pontus'. PG 46.962C-964A.

lived.text: Most of her life at Annesi, the family estate on the river Iris in Pontus, near Neocaesarea. The Iris is today's Yeşilırmak, in northern Turkey. There she and her mother turned the household into a community of women.
lived.source: Clarke, introduction: 'the family estate at Annesi, near Neo-Caesarea'; 'At Annesi, on the opposite side of the river, his mother Emmelia and sister Macrina were living on the family estate.' NCE: 'd. by the river Iris in Pontus'. ToposText: 'Iris, River of Pontus, the modern Yeşilırmak'.
lived.note: The Life itself names the Iris (in the story of Naucratius) but never uses the name Annesi. The spelling varies: Annesi, Annisa. The exact modern site is not known for certain (not checked).

died.text: In 379 or 380, of a fever, at her community on the Iris. Her brother Gregory was with her. He says he came nine months or more after Basil's death, on his way home from a synod at Antioch.
died.source: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Gregory resolves to visit his sister' ('It was the ninth month or a little longer after this disaster, and a synod of bishops was gathered at Antioch') and 'Gregory comes to the monastery' ('her strength being already drained by fever'). NCE: 'd. by the river Iris in Pontus, December of 379 or 380.' Catholic Encyclopedia (1910): 'died 379'; 'On his return from a synod of Antioch, towards the end of 379'. OCA and azbyka.ru: 380. Clarke's introduction: 'On January 1, 379, Basil died; in September of the same year Gregory attended a Council at Antioch'.
died.note: No ancient text gives a day. The churches keep 19 July, and Wikipedia prints 'died 19 July 379', but if Basil died on 1 January 379 (Clarke's date), nine months later is autumn 379, which is why the NCE says December 379 or 380. Some scholars date Basil's death to 378, which would fit July 379 (not checked in a scholarly source). Plain wording: 'She died in 379 or 380.'

buried.text: In the family grave, beside her mother, in the chapel of the Holy Martyrs, seven or eight stades (about a mile) from her community. Gregory and the local bishop, Araxius, carried the bier.
buried.source: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Gregory makes the funeral arrangements' and 'The family grave is opened': 'Seven or eight stades intervened between the Retreat and the abode of the Holy Martyrs, in which also the bodies of our parents were laid.'; 'took up that holy body from the bed and laid it down by the side of the mother'; 'Araxius by name'.
buried.note: A stade is about 185 m, so 7 or 8 stades is roughly 1.3 to 1.5 km, 'about a mile'. The conversion is ours.

also_called.text: The Teacher: Gregory's name for her in his dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection.
also_called.source: On the Soul and the Resurrection, opening: 'But his sister the Teacher was still living'
also_called.note: The dialogue itself was also known as the 'Macrinia' (Catholic Encyclopedia 1910: 'Hence the title of the work, ta Makrinia'; NCE: 'Gregory's Macrinia').

also_called.text: Thecla: a secret name. Before she was born, her mother dreamed that a shining figure called the baby Thecla, after the famous virgin follower of St Paul.
also_called.source: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Macrina's parents' and 'The birth of Macrina': 'another name had been given her privately, as the result of a vision before she was born into the world'; 'addressed the child she was carrying by the name of Thecla'.
also_called.note: 'Now this name was used only in secret.'

also_called.text: Venerable Macrina (Orthodox; 'Venerable' is the title for monastic saints). Greek: Οσία Μακρίνα, αδελφή του Μεγάλου Βασιλείου. Russian: Преподобная Макрина Каппадокийская, Новая, Младшая (Macrina of Cappadocia, the New, the Younger).
also_called.source: OCA, 'Venerable Macrina, sister of Saint Basil the Great'; saint.gr page 728; azbyka.ru
Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, 19 July: 'Macrina of Caesarea, Monastic and Teacher, 379'

also_called.text: Macrina the Younger, to tell her from her grandmother, Macrina the Elder.
also_called.source: NCE, 'Macrina, Ss.' (both women in one entry); Catholic Encyclopedia (1910)

roles.name: Daughter at home
roles.line: Stayed with her mother after her fiancé died
roles.text: Betrothed at about twelve, she treated the betrothal as a marriage when the young man died, and resolved never to leave her mother.
roles.source: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Her betrothal', 'Death of the young man' and 'Macrina resolves never to leave her mother'

roles.name: Teacher of her brothers
roles.line: Raised Peter and turned Basil round
roles.text: She raised her youngest brother Peter herself, 'father, teacher, tutor, mother'. She took Basil in hand when he came home proud of his speaking.
roles.source: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Basil returns from the University' and 'Peter, the youngest brother'

roles.name: Head of a community
roles.line: Of women on the river Iris
roles.text: She drew her mother and the household maids into one community of prayer and work. After her mother died she led it. Gregory calls her the abbess; the men's side was led by Peter.
roles.source: Life of Macrina ('I guessed the explanation, that the abbess was not with them'; the soldier's story: 'the men's department, presided over by Peter, your brother'); Clarke, introduction: 'a double monastery, the men presided over by Peter, the women by Macrina'
roles.note: NCE: 'superior of one of the earliest communities of women ascetics'.

roles.name: The Teacher
roles.line: On her deathbed, in Gregory's dialogue
roles.text: In the dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection, Gregory writes up their last conversation, with her as 'the Teacher'.
roles.source: On the Soul and the Resurrection, opening; Life of Macrina, footnote 6 in Clarke: 'In the long dialogue, De Anima et Resurrectione ... Gregory purports to reproduce this conversation.'

status.text: A saint to Catholics and Orthodox. The Church of England and the Episcopal Church keep her day. The ELCA remembers her with the Cappadocian Fathers. The Missouri Synod does not list her.

patron_of.text: No patronage found in a reliable source. Leave the row out.
patron_of.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), NCE, OCA, LFF 2022: none names one.
patron_of.note: Wikidata lists no patronage for her (wd-patron.json has no entry).

in_art.text: In the East: a veiled woman in a dark cloak, with a halo, both hands raised with the palms outward (the 11th-century fresco in St Sophia, Kyiv).
in_art.source: The fresco itself (Wikimedia Commons, 'Macrina the Younger.jpg')
in_art.note: Described from the picture, not from a reference work on iconography. CHECKER 2026-09-25: the page no longer says "In the East" or "No fixed symbol": one fresco does not show an Eastern type, and no source states the absence of a symbol. The page names the Kyiv fresco and the Rome statue only.

in_art.text: In the West: as a young woman looking up, one hand on her breast and a book in the other (the 1668 statue on the colonnade of St Peter's Square), or as a nun in a black veil holding a cross (a Barcelona devotional print of 1870).
in_art.source: Photograph by Alf van Beem (CC0); stpetersbasilica.info, 'St Macrina - Colonnade Saints' (statue 21: 'The right hand is on her chest and the left is holding a book'); BnF Gallica goigs sheet, Barcelona, Lluís Tasso, 1870
in_art.note: No reference work gives her a fixed attribute. Plain wording that holds: 'Usually as a veiled nun. There is no fixed symbol.'

wrote.text: Nothing that survives. Everything we have of her comes through her brother Gregory of Nyssa.
wrote.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, 19 July: 'Macrina left no writings; we know of her through the works of her brother, Gregory of Nyssa.' NCE on the dialogue: 'While the theological views are undoubtedly Gregory's, it is revealing that he can represent her with verisimilitude as so learned.'

pronounced.text: mah-KREE-nuh (proposed; NOT confirmed in a dictionary).
pronounced.source: No entry found in Merriam-Webster (404), Dictionary.com (redirects to 'marina'), Wiktionary (404) or the Century Cyclopedia of Names (1903, which has only the emperor 'Macrinus (ma-kri'nus)'). Collins blocked the checker (403). Name sites (Forvo, HowToPronounce) give 'mah-KREE-nuh' but are not dictionaries.
pronounced.note: Leave the 'Pronounced' row out until a dictionary or reference pronouncing guide confirms it. The Greek is Μακρίνα (ma-KREE-na); an older English habit, following Latin 'Macrinus', could say ma-KRY-na.

catholic.text: 19 July, in the Roman Martyrology. She is not on the General Roman Calendar, so there is no Mass for her in most parishes.
catholic.source: The Roman Martyrology (1916 English edition), 19 July: 'In Cappadocia, the holy virgin Marcina, sister of St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory of Nyssa.' The 1956 Latin edition, 19 July: 'In Cappadocia sanctae Macrinae Virginis, filiae sanctorum Basilii et Emmeliae, atque sororis item sanctorum Episcoporum Basilii Magni, Gregorii Nysseni et Petri Sebastensis.' NCE: 'Feast: July 19.' General Roman Calendar for July: nothing on 19 July (20 July is St Apollinaris).
catholic.note: The 1916 scan prints 'Marcina' (a misprint or scan error; its own index lists 'Macrina, St., V July 19'). The 1956 text was read on a blog transcription (martirologioromano1956.blogspot.com), not a scan. The current (2004) Martyrology was NOT checked. The General Roman Calendar was checked on Wikipedia's list only (USCCB returned 403).

orthodox.text: 19 July. The Greek churches and the OCA keep 19 July. The Russian Church keeps 19 July on the old calendar, which is 1 August on today's calendar.
orthodox.source: saint.gr, 'Οσία Μακρίνα αδελφή του Μεγάλου Βασιλείου': 'Εορτάζει στις 19 Ιουλίου εκάστου έτους.' OCA, 'Venerable Macrina, sister of Saint Basil the Great', on its 19 July page. azbyka.ru, 'Преподобная Макрина Каппадокийская': 'День памяти 1 августа'.
orthodox.note: GOARCH returned 403 (not checked). Unlike Martin, 'East' here is one date: 19 July everywhere, shown on the civil calendar as 1 August by churches on the old calendar.

old_calendar_note.text: Churches on the old (Julian) calendar keep 19 July thirteen days later, on 1 August.
old_calendar_note.source: azbyka.ru gives 1 August for the Russian Church.

anglican.text: 19 July, with her brother: 'Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, and his sister Macrina, Deaconess, Teachers of the Faith'. A Lesser Festival in the Church of England. The Episcopal Church keeps 19 July too: 'Macrina of Caesarea, Monastic and Teacher, 379'.
anglican.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar: '19 Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, and his sister Macrina, Deaconess, Teachers of the Faith, c.394 and c.379', printed in roman type ('Lesser Festivals are printed in ordinary roman typeface'). Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, calendar for July and pages 312-313.
anglican.note: The Episcopal Church keeps Gregory of Nyssa separately, on 9 March (LFF 2022, page 128).

lutheran.text: ELCA: 14 June, with the Cappadocian Fathers ('Macrina, theologian, c. 379'). The Missouri Synod's Lutheran Service Book does not list her; it keeps Basil and the two Gregorys on 10 January.
lutheran.source: Evangelical Lutheran Worship, The Church Year, final draft January 2006 (ELCA, archived): '14 Basil the Great, Bishop of Caesarea, 379 W / Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, c. 385 W / Gregory of Nazianzus, Bishop of Constantinople, c. 389 W / Macrina, theologian, c. 379 W'. LSB commemorations lists (goodshepherd.nb.ca; CPH blog): 10 January 'Basil the Great of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa, Pastors and Confessors', no Macrina.
lutheran.note: The ELCA line is from the final draft, not the printed book (the same document Martin's ELCA date was checked in). In ELW, commemorations are printed in roman type.

why_dates_differ.text: 19 July is the day the Greek and Roman calendars kept. The ELCA puts her on 14 June so the family is remembered together, on the old Western day of St Basil.
why_dates_differ.source: ELW draft (14 June grouping); Wikidata gives Basil's old Roman date as 14 June (wd dumps, unverified).
why_dates_differ.note: No source states WHY the ELCA chose 14 June; that 14 June is Basil's traditional Western day is from Wikidata and memory, not checked. Print only the dates, not the reason.

lines: Her father chose the young man
numbers.text: She was betrothed in her twelfth year; the young man died soon after.
numbers.source: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'Her betrothal' ('the growing girl reached her twelfth year'); Catholic Encyclopedia (1910): 'When she was but twelve years old, her father had already arranged a marriage for her'
numbers.note: Strictly, 'her twelfth year' means aged 11. 'About 12' is safest.

numbers.text: Her parents had ten children; four sons and five daughters survived infancy. Macrina was the eldest.
numbers.source: Clarke, introduction: 'His parents, Basil and Emmelia, had ten children, of whom four sons and five daughters survived infancy. The eldest child, Macrina'. Life: 'the earliest born of my mother's womb'. NPNF 2nd series vol. 8, prolegomena: 'ten children, five boys and five girls'.

numbers.text: Three of her brothers became bishops: Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nyssa and Peter of Sebaste.
numbers.source: NPNF 2nd series vol. 8 (Basil), prolegomena: 'The three remaining brothers occupied respectively the sees of Cæsarea, Nyssa, and Sebasteia.'
numbers.note: The line 'Two are Church Fathers' is our wording (Basil and Gregory of Nyssa are both counted among the Cappadocian Fathers, LFF 2022 p. 128). The CCEL chapter URL for the prolegomena was not opened; the text was checked in the CCEL plain-text volume. CHECKER 2026-09-25: the old URL npnf208.iv.html is the Genealogical Tables page; the prolegomena line ("sees of Cæsarea, Nyssa, and Sebasteia") is on npnf208.vi.i.i.html (Life: Parentage and Birth), opened and found.

numbers.text: Troubles and exile kept Gregory away 'no less than eight years, or very nearly'.
numbers.source: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'Gregory resolves to visit his sister'

numbers.text: Gregory's visit came 'the ninth month or a little longer' after Basil's death.
numbers.source: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'Gregory resolves to visit his sister'
numbers.note: Use either this or 'Years apart', not both, if space is short.

traits.title: steady in a disaster
traits.text: When her favourite brother Naucratius was killed, her mother collapsed. Macrina did not. She held her mother up and talked her through it.
traits.quote_exact: Facing the disaster in a rational spirit, she both preserved herself from collapse, and becoming the prop of her mother's weakness, raised her up from the abyss of grief, and by her own steadfastness and imperturbability taught her mother's soul to be brave.
traits.source: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'Macrina the one support of her mother' (PG 46.970A)
traits.note: 'For it was a brother, and a favourite brother, who had been snatched away' (same part).

traits.title: blunt with her brothers
traits.text: Basil came home 'puffed up beyond measure with the pride of oratory', and she took him in hand. When Gregory poured out his troubles on her deathbed, she told him to stop complaining and count his blessings.
traits.quote_exact: Will you not cease to be insensible to the divine blessings? Will you not remedy the ingratitude of your soul?
traits.source: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Basil returns from the University' (PG 46.966C) and 'Gregory returns to Macrina, who recalls the events of her childhood' (PG 46.982A)
traits.note: She went on: 'it is your parents' prayers that are lifting you up on high, you that have little or no equipment within yourself for such success?' (exact).

traits.title: kept nothing
traits.text: She gave her whole share of the family property to the Church. When she died, there were no burial clothes to find. The deaconess Lampadia told Gregory her wealth was a cloak, a head-covering and a pair of worn shoes.
traits.quote_exact: There is the cloak, there is the head-covering, there the well-worn shoes on the feet. This is all her wealth, these are her riches.
traits.source: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Gregory returns to Macrina' ('all her share was given into the priest's hands according to the divine command') and 'Vestiana comes to help Gregory' (Lampadia's words)

traits.title: cheerful to the end
traits.text: Dying of fever, she hid how hard it was to breathe so as not to upset her brother. She led the talk and asked him questions.
traits.quote_exact: Lest she should vex my soul she stilled her groans and made great efforts to hide, if possible, the difficulty of her breathing. And in every way she tried to be cheerful, both taking the lead herself in friendly talk, and giving us an opportunity by asking questions.
traits.source: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'Gregory comes to the monastery and finds Macrina on her death bed' (PG 46.978A)

traits.title: treated the maids as sisters (spare)
traits.text: She persuaded her mother to live as an equal with the maids: the same food, the same kind of bed.
traits.quote_exact: She induced her to live on a footing of equality with the staff of maids, so as to share with them in the same food, the same kind of bed, and in all the necessaries of life, without any regard to differences of rank.
traits.source: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'Mother and daughter make further progress in the ascetic life' (PG 46.970C)
traits.note: Also: 'treating all her slave girls and menials as if they were sisters and belonged to the same rank as herself' (PG 46.966D). The household had slaves; Clarke does not say they were freed (see could_not_verify).

traits.title: a mother to the abandoned (spare)
traits.text: In a famine she picked up babies left to die by the roadside and raised them. At her death they mourned her as their mother.
traits.quote_exact: These were they whom she picked up, exposed by the roadside in the time of famine.
traits.source: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'The sisters' lament for their abbess' (PG 46.988B)
traits.note: 'Saddest of all in their grief were those who called on her as mother and nurse.'

lede.text: Almost everything we know comes from one brother. Gregory of Nyssa wrote her Life soon after she died, from what he saw himself and what her nuns told him.
lede.source: Life of Macrina, introduction: 'Our account of her was not based on the narrative of others, but our talk was an accurate description of what we had learned by personal experience'; Clarke's introduction: 'written down shortly after their occurrence'.
lede.note: NCE: Gregory wrote it 'at the request of the monk Olympus' (the Life is headed 'To the monk Olympius'). No other writer of her time describes her; Basil's letters never name her (see family).

quotes.exact: Store-cupboard indeed!" said she; "you have in front of you all her treasure. There is the cloak, there is the head-covering, there the well-worn shoes on the feet. This is all her wealth, these are her riches.
quotes.who: Lampadia, the deaconess who led the sisters, when Gregory asked for burial clothes
quotes.place: the part headed 'Vestiana comes to help Gregory' (PG 46.990A)
quotes.note: She goes on: 'She knew of one store-house alone for her wealth, the treasure in heaven.' (exact)

quotes.exact: Learn what manner of goodness has been taken away from human life.
quotes.who: A soldier from Sebastopolis, a relative, meeting Gregory on the road home from the funeral
quotes.place: the part headed 'The funeral over, Gregory returns home' (PG 46.996C)

quotes.exact: The light of our eyes has gone out,
quotes.place: the part headed 'The sisters' lament for their abbess' (PG 46.988A)
quotes.note: The lament continues 'The light that guided our souls has been taken away.' Printed as verse lines in Clarke.

quotes.exact: her mother would often say that she had carried the rest of her children in her womb for a definite time, but that Macrina she bore always
quotes.who: Her mother, Emmelia, as Gregory reports it
quotes.place: the part headed 'Macrina resolves never to leave her mother' (PG 46.964D)

life_moments.title: One marriage
life_moments.text: Her father chose a young man of good family, a rising speaker in the law courts. He died before the wedding. Macrina said her father's plan counted as a marriage. There is one marriage, she said, as there is one birth and one death. Her fiancé was not dead but away, living to God. She turned down every other suitor.
life_moments.quote_exact: since in the nature of things there was but one marriage, as there is one birth and one death
life_moments.cite: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Her betrothal' and 'Death of the young man' (PG 46.964B-D)
life_moments.note: Reported speech ('she would say that...'), not her words verbatim.

life_moments.title: Never leaving her mother
life_moments.text: She resolved never to leave her mother, even for a moment. She cooked her mother's meals with her own hands and helped run estates in three provinces. She raised her baby brother Peter herself.
life_moments.quote_exact: Thus having become all things to the lad---- father, teacher, tutor, mother, giver of all good advice
life_moments.cite: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Macrina resolves never to leave her mother' and 'Peter, the youngest brother' (PG 46.964D-966B, 972B-C)
life_moments.note: 'paid taxes to three different governors, since her property was scattered in as many districts' (the mother's property). Clarke prints a long dash as four hyphens.

life_moments.title: Basil comes home
life_moments.text: Basil came back from his studies, already a practised speaker, full of himself. He looked down on the leading men of the district. Macrina took him in hand. He gave up his fame, gave away his property and took up a life of work with his hands.
life_moments.quote_exact: He was puffed up beyond measure with the pride of oratory and looked down on the local dignitaries
life_moments.cite: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'Basil returns from the University' (PG 46.966C)
life_moments.note: The year is not in the Life. NPNF vol. 8 prolegomena put Basil's baptism about 357, 'To the same period' as his turn to the ascetic life. Safer 'when' label: 'When Basil came home'. Basil's own account of this turn (Letter 223) does not mention her.

life_moments.title: A brother killed
life_moments.text: Naucratius, the brother next after Basil, lived as a hermit on the Iris and fished to feed poor old people. He was brought home dead from one of those trips, with his servant Chrysapius. Their mother collapsed. Macrina held her up.
life_moments.quote_exact: by her own steadfastness and imperturbability taught her mother's soul to be brave
life_moments.cite: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'The story of Naucratius', 'The tragic death of Naucratius' and 'Macrina the one support of her mother' (PG 46.966D-970B)
life_moments.note: The Life does not say it was a hunting accident; it says only that he died on one of his food-gathering 'expeditions' with no previous illness. Clarke's introduction says 'killed on a hunting expedition'.

life_moments.title: Mistress and maids as sisters
life_moments.text: She led her mother to give up her grand way of living. Mother, daughter and maids shared the same food and the same beds, and prayed and sang day and night. In a famine, crowds came for food. Macrina picked up babies abandoned by the roadside and raised them.
life_moments.quote_exact: She induced her to live on a footing of equality with the staff of maids, so as to share with them in the same food, the same kind of bed, and in all the necessaries of life, without any regard to differences of rank.
life_moments.cite: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Mother and daughter make further progress in the ascetic life', 'Peter, the youngest brother' and 'The sisters' lament for their abbess'
life_moments.note: Emmelia later died 'in the arms of her two children', Macrina and Peter, blessing them as her 'first-fruits' and 'tenth' (exact: 'yielding up her life in the arms of her two children').

life_moments.title: Gregory's last visit
life_moments.text: Nine months after Basil died, Gregory came, after nearly eight years away. He found her lying on a board on the floor, burning with fever. She raised herself on one elbow to greet him. They talked about Basil, the soul and the resurrection. When he poured out his own troubles, she told him to be grateful instead.
life_moments.quote_exact: This favour also Thou hast granted me, O God, and hast not deprived me of my desire, because Thou hast stirred up Thy servant to visit Thy handmaid.
life_moments.cite: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Gregory resolves to visit his sister' to 'Gregory returns to Macrina' (PG 46.974C-982C)
life_moments.note: On the way, Gregory dreamed three times of carrying martyrs' relics that shone like a mirror in the sun.

life_moments.title: Her last prayer
life_moments.text: She turned her bed to the East and stopped talking to them. She prayed aloud until her voice gave out. When the lamps were lit, she tried to join the evening thanksgiving with her lips and hands. Then she made the sign of the cross, drew one deep breath, and died.
life_moments.quote_exact: she drew a great deep breath and closed her life and her prayer together
life_moments.cite: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Macrina's dying prayer' (PG 46.984B-986B)

lede.text: Gregory tells two healings in full and names more he chose to leave out, because people would not believe them.
lede.quote_exact: But what exceeds the capacity of the hearer, men receive with insult and suspicion of falsehood, as remote from truth.
lede.cite: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'Conclusion' (PG 46.1000A)
lede.note: This is the 'doubted from the start' line, in the source's own words: Gregory himself says wonders are received 'with insult and suspicion of falsehood'.

items.title: The tumour
items.place: At home, while her mother lived
items.who_saw: Told to Gregory by Vestiana, a widow in the community, over Macrina's body. She showed him the scar by lamplight.
items.text: A growth appeared on her chest, below the neck, and it threatened to spread toward the heart. Her mother begged her to see a doctor, but Macrina thought showing her body to a stranger was worse than the pain. She prayed all night in the sanctuary, weeping, and put the mud from her tears on the sore. Then she asked her mother to make the sign of the cross on it. The tumour went. A tiny scar was left, like the mark of a needle.
items.quote_exact: But when the mother put her hand within her bosom, to make the sign of the cross on the part, the sign worked and the tumour disappeared.
items.cite: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'They find on the body marks of Macrina's sanctity' (PG 46.990D-992C)
items.note: The mother's side, in her own words as reported: 'the medical art, she said, was sent from God for the saving of men.' Tell this as the source tells it, and never as advice about medical care. The speaker is 'the sister who shared with me that great inheritance' = Vestiana (she took the cross, Gregory the ring). The Life says 'a small faint mark below the neck'; the Greek word for where the growth was is rendered 'bosom'/'breast' region by Clarke ('put her hand within her bosom').

items.title: The little girl's eye
items.place: At her community; the family lived at Sebastopolis
items.who_saw: The girl's father, a soldier in command at Sebastopolis and a relative, told Gregory on his way home. His wife was there.
items.text: The family visited the community. Macrina held their little daughter, who had a whitish growth on one eye after an illness, and kissed her eyes. She promised them a medicine for the eye if they stayed to eat. On the way home they realised they had forgotten it. Then the mother looked at the child. The eye was healed.
items.quote_exact: She has indeed given her the true drug which cures disease; it is the healing that comes from prayer.
items.cite: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'The soldier's story' (PG 46.996D-998D)
items.note: The father: 'I understood the marvels of the Gospel that hitherto had been incredible to me' (exact: 'the marvels of the Gospel that hitherto had been incredible to me'). He wept as he told it.

items.title: Grain that did not run out
items.place: At her community, in a famine
items.who_saw: People who lived with her, Gregory says. He heard it; he did not see it.
items.text: In the famine, grain was handed out to the hungry again and again, and the heap never got smaller.
items.quote_exact: the corn for the relief of need, though constantly distributed, suffered no perceptible diminution, remaining always in bulk the same as before it was distributed to the needs of the suppliants
items.cite: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'Conclusion' (PG 46.1000A)
items.note: Gregory mentions it only to say he is leaving it out: 'Consequently I omit that extraordinary agricultural operation in the famine time'.

items.title: More he left out
items.who_saw: Those 'who lived with her and knew her life accurately'
items.text: Gregory adds that people who knew her told of healings, demons cast out and true predictions. He left them out on purpose.
items.quote_exact: Healings of diseases, and castings out of demons, and true predictions of the future.
items.cite: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'Conclusion' (PG 46.1000A)
items.note: 'All are believed to be true, even though apparently incredible, by those who have investigated them accurately.'

items.title: Light from her body (optional)
items.text: On his way, Gregory dreamed three times that he carried martyrs' relics shining like a mirror in the sun. When her body was laid out in her mother's dark robe, he says it seemed to shine, as in his dream.
items.quote_exact: rays actually seemed to shine forth from her beauty
items.cite: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Gregory comes to the monastery' and 'They find on the body marks of Macrina's sanctity' (PG 46.976B, 992D)
items.note: Gregory's own wording is careful: 'as I think', 'seemed'. Keep 'seemed'.

items.title: A name in a dream (optional)
items.text: In labour, her mother dreamed that a figure more splendid than a human being called the baby Thecla three times. Then the birth was easy.
items.quote_exact: addressed the child she was carrying by the name of Thecla
items.cite: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'The birth of Macrina' (PG 46.962B)

relic.text: Round her neck they found an iron cross and an iron ring. The ring was hollow and held, they said, a tiny piece of the True Cross. Gregory kept the ring and Vestiana the cross.
relic.quote_exact: a particle of the Cross of Life
relic.cite: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'They find on the body marks of Macrina's sanctity' (PG 46.990C-D)
relic.note: A tidbit, not a miracle. NPNF vol. 5 prolegomena tell it too.

doubt.text: Gregory expected doubt. He says he left most of the wonders out 'lest the unbeliever should be injured by being led to disbelieve the gifts of God'. The soldier himself says the Gospel miracles had been 'incredible' to him until that day.
doubt.quote_exact: lest the unbeliever should be injured by being led to disbelieve the gifts of God
doubt.cite: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'The soldier's story' and 'Conclusion'
doubt.note: No named early doubter is recorded, unlike Martin's.

framing.text: Macrina wrote nothing that survives. These are her words as her brother Gregory recorded them: in his Life of Macrina, and in his dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection, where the views are his own in her voice.
framing.source: LFF 2022 ('Macrina left no writings'); NCE ('While the theological views are undoubtedly Gregory's, it is revealing that he can represent her with verisimilitude as so learned.')
framing.note: Say which work each line comes from. Lines from the Life are Gregory's memory of what she said; lines from the dialogue are a literary composition.

feature.exact: Thou, O Lord, hast freed us from the fear of death. Thou hast made the end of this life the beginning to us of true life.
feature.display: Thou, O Lord, hast freed us from the fear of death. Thou hast made the end of this life the beginning to us of true life.
feature.ctx: The opening of the prayer she said on her deathbed, facing the East, as Gregory heard it.
feature.note: Capitals already as printed. The Greek original was NOT found in a free source (see could_not_verify); print the English only. Suggested ghost word: 'vita' is Latin and wrong here; use none, or the English 'life'.

lines.display: Will you not cease to be insensible to the divine blessings? Will you not remedy the ingratitude of your soul?

misquoted_or_legend.claim: She suffered in the persecutions and was taught by Gregory the Wonderworker.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: That was her grandmother, Macrina the Elder. The grandmother is kept on 14 January, the granddaughter on 19 July.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Roman Martyrology (1916), 14 January: 'St. Macrina, disciple of St. Gregory Thaumaturgus, and grandmother of St. Basil, whom she brought up in the Christian faith.' Life of Macrina: named 'after a famous Macrina some time before in the family, our father's mother, who had confessed Christ like a good athlete in the time of the persecutions'. NCE: Macrina the Elder, 'disciple of gregory thaumaturgus', feast 14 January.
misquoted_or_legend.note: The research file warned that the two are often confused online.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: Her writings, or her book On the Soul and the Resurrection.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: She wrote nothing that survives. The dialogue is Gregory's, written in her voice. The New Catholic Encyclopedia says its views are 'undoubtedly Gregory's'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: NCE, 'Macrina, Ss.'; LFF 2022, 19 July ('Macrina left no writings')

misquoted_or_legend.claim: She died in her brother's arms.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Gregory does not say so. He says she prayed until her voice failed, made the sign of the cross and breathed her last. Then he laid her hands on her face, as she had asked. It was their mother who died in the arms of her two children, Macrina and Peter.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'Macrina's dying prayer', 'Gregory performs the last offices' and 'Death of the mother' ('yielding up her life in the arms of her two children'). The claim is in LFF 2022, page 128: 'Macrina died in her brother's arms.'

misquoted_or_legend.claim: The nuns told Gregory how she healed a little girl's eye.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: The girl's father told him, a soldier from Sebastopolis whom Gregory met on the road home.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Life of Macrina, the parts headed 'The funeral over, Gregory returns home' and 'The soldier's story'. The claim is on the OCA's page ('told by the sisters of the monastery to Saint Gregory of Nyssa') and on azbyka.ru.
misquoted_or_legend.note: The OCA page has a second slip: it says 'Another daughter was named Macrina', as if Thecla and Macrina were two daughters. In the Life they are two names of the same girl.

misquoted_or_legend.truth: The Church of England's calendar calls her one. Gregory never does. In his Life the deaconess is Lampadia, 'leader of the band of sisters'. He calls Macrina the abbess.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Church of England Common Worship calendar, 19 July ('Macrina, Deaconess'); Life of Macrina ('a lady called Lampadia, leader of the band of sisters, a deaconess in rank'; 'the abbess was not with them')
misquoted_or_legend.note: Word this gently: say what Gregory's Life does and does not say, not that the Church of England is wrong. Some scholars may argue she held the office (not checked).

misquoted_or_legend.claim: Basil took his mother and sister to the family estate on the Iris.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Gregory tells it the other way round. Macrina drew Basil into the ascetic life, and she and her mother were living at Annesi when he began his own monastery across the river.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) has the claim ('On the death of their father, Basil took her, with their mother, to a family estate on the River Iris'). Against it: Life of Macrina, 'Basil returns from the University'; Clarke, introduction ('At Annesi, on the opposite side of the river, his mother Emmelia and sister Macrina were living on the family estate').
misquoted_or_legend.note: Spare; the weakest of the six.

where_she_stood.text: Eight of the quiz's 23 statements; six show a line (all through Gregory) and two are scored but hidden ('learning', 'mystery'). Values from site/src/data/which-early-christian.json, people.macrina.cells. Every shown line was found word for word.

rows.statement: Anger at real wrongdoing can be a good thing.
rows.line: But, whenever their impulse is towards what is noble, then they become matter for praise, as his desire did to Daniel, and his anger to Phineas, and their grief to those who nobly mourn.
rows.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
rows.place: the part on the passions, about a third of the way in (Macrina speaking, after 'And who, she replied, could deny...')

rows.statement: If someone you know is doing wrong, it's your job to tell them.
rows.line: Will you not cease to be insensible to the divine blessings? Will you not remedy the ingratitude of your soul?
rows.place: the part headed 'Gregory returns to Macrina, who recalls the events of her childhood' (PG 46.982A)

rows.statement: Even if you believe you'll see them again, it's right to weep openly for someone you've lost.
rows.line: She quoted the Apostle's words about the duty of not being grieved for them that sleep; because only men without hope have such feelings.
rows.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
rows.note: Exact in New Advent. CCEL prints inner quotation marks: 'not being "grieved for them that sleep"; because only "men without hope"'. The words are Gregory's report of her, as the cell's 'by' already says. She quotes 1 Thessalonians 4:13.

rows.statement: The best way to live is free of strong emotions, with only a steady peace inside.
rows.line: It will therefore be no detriment to our participation in the Good, that the soul should be free from such emotions.
rows.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
rows.place: about halfway, on desire and the purified soul (Macrina speaking: 'To that objection, she replied...')
rows.note: Cut short with a full stop; in the source a comma follows ('emotions, and turning back upon herself...'). Context: she speaks of the soul freed from passions 'whether by forethought here, or by purgation hereafter', so the line is about this life and the next.

rows.statement: In many Bible stories, the deeper meaning matters more than the history.
rows.line: It is impossible to make the framework of the narrative correspond with the truth, if we understand it literally; we can do that only by translating each detail into an equivalent in the world of ideas.
rows.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
rows.place: a little before halfway, on the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16)
rows.note: The source begins 'and so it is impossible...' (lower case); the site capitalises the first word. She is speaking of one parable, not of Bible stories in general.

rows.statement: In the end, God will save everyone.
rows.line: But He that becomes all things will be in all things too; and herein it appears to me that Scripture teaches the complete annihilation of evil.
rows.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
rows.place: a little past halfway, on 1 Corinthians 15:28
rows.note: Exact in New Advent; CCEL prints "all" and "in all" in quotation marks, with a footnote mark after 'evil'.

rows.statement: Wisdom is worth learning from anyone, even people who don't share your faith.
rows.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
rows.note: Hidden in the data (hide: true). Not re-checked.

rows.statement: Some questions about God are better left alone.
rows.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
rows.note: Hidden in the data (hide: true). Not re-checked.

family_friends_rivals.name: Basil the Great
family_friends_rivals.text: He came home from his studies proud of his speaking, and she turned him to a life of poverty and work. In his own letters he never names her.
family_friends_rivals.source: Life of Macrina, 'Basil returns from the University'. Basil, Letter 223 (NPNF vol. 8): his account of his turn from 'vanity' names no one, and he credits his faith to 'my blessed mother and my grandmother Macrina'. A search of all 354 letters in NPNF vol. 8 finds 'Macrina' only for the grandmother.
family_friends_rivals.note: Exact from Letter 223: 'The teaching about God which I had received as a boy from my blessed mother and my grandmother Macrina, I have ever held with increased conviction.' NPNF vol. 8 is not quite complete (366 letters are usually counted); say 'in his letters that survive in the standard English edition' or simply 'his letters never name her' after a check of the Greek list.

family_friends_rivals.name: Gregory of Nyssa
family_friends_rivals.text: He wrote her Life and the dialogue that makes her 'the Teacher'. He sat with her as she died, laid her hands over her eyes as she had asked, and helped carry her bier.
family_friends_rivals.source: Life of Macrina; On the Soul and the Resurrection
family_friends_rivals.note: 'I got under the bed and called Araxius to the other side' (the bier).

family_friends_rivals.name: Peter of Sebaste
family_friends_rivals.text: Born as their father died, he was raised by Macrina. He later led the men's side of the community and became bishop of Sebaste.
family_friends_rivals.source: Life of Macrina, 'Peter, the youngest brother'; the soldier's story ('the men's department, presided over by Peter'); NPNF vol. 8 prolegomena (Sebasteia)
family_friends_rivals.note: Peter was away when Gregory arrived, having gone to meet him by another road.

family_friends_rivals.name: Naucratius
family_friends_rivals.text: The most gifted of the brothers, he left a brilliant start to live as a hermit on the Iris, caring for poor old people. He died suddenly on one of his trips.
family_friends_rivals.source: Life of Macrina, 'The story of Naucratius'

family_friends_rivals.name: Emmelia
family_friends_rivals.text: Macrina never left her. Emmelia pleaded with her to see a doctor, and in the end lived as an equal with her own maids. She died in the arms of Macrina and Peter.
family_friends_rivals.note: OCA keeps St Emmelia on 1 January (per the OCA Macrina page: 'Saint Emilia (January 1)').

family_friends_rivals.name: Macrina the Elder
family_friends_rivals.text: Her father's mother, who confessed Christ in the persecutions. Macrina was named after her.
family_friends_rivals.source: Life of Macrina, 'Macrina's parents'; Roman Martyrology (1916), 14 January

family_friends_rivals.name: Lampadia and Vestiana
family_friends_rivals.text: Lampadia, a deaconess, led the sisters. Vestiana, a young senator's daughter widowed early, had put herself under Macrina's care. They laid out her body with Gregory.
family_friends_rivals.source: Life of Macrina, 'Vestiana comes to help Gregory'
family_friends_rivals.note: Clarke: Vestiana's 'father was one of those who composed the council of senators'.

how_she_died.text: Of a fever, in 379 or 380, at her community on the Iris, with her brother Gregory beside her. She lay on a sack spread on a board on the floor. On her last day she turned her bed to the East and prayed aloud until her voice gave out. At the lighting of the lamps she tried to join the evening thanksgiving with her lips and hands. She made the sign of the cross and died with one deep breath. Her nuns broke into loud weeping. She was buried beside her mother the next day, after an all-night vigil with psalms.
how_she_died.source: Life of Macrina, from 'Gregory comes to the monastery' to 'The family grave is opened'
how_she_died.note: Exact lines: 'She was lying not on a bed or couch, but on the floor; a sack had been spread on a board'; 'Her couch had been turned towards the East'; 'she drew a great deep breath and closed her life and her prayer together'. No later legend was found.

is_she_a_saint.text: Yes, to Catholics and Orthodox. Catholics list her in the Roman Martyrology on 19 July, though she is not on the General Roman Calendar. The Orthodox keep her on 19 July as a 'venerable' (monastic) saint. The Church of England and the Episcopal Church keep her day too. The ELCA remembers her with the Cappadocian Fathers on 14 June. Her cult began in the East right after her death and reached the West late.
is_she_a_saint.source: Roman Martyrology 1916 and 1956; OCA; saint.gr; azbyka.ru; Church of England Common Worship; LFF 2022; ELW 2006 draft; LSB lists; NCE: 'An unusual number of manuscripts of this biography coming from the environs of Pontus suggest a strong local cult after 379, which spread through the East in the Greek, Egyptian, Syrian, and Arab Churches ... Her cult in the West is late since the life was not translated into Latin until the 16th century.'
is_she_a_saint.note: Gregory himself calls her 'the saint' throughout the Life. The Missouri Synod does not list her. She was never 'canonized' by a process; like all saints of her time she was honoured before such processes existed (our wording, not a source's).

hard_topics.text: In Gregory's dialogue, Macrina teaches that God will be 'all in all' and evil will be wholly destroyed, and that the fire after death heals rather than only punishes. Holders read this as hope for all. Critics later linked it with Origen. Gregory was never condemned. In the eighth century Patriarch Germanus of Constantinople argued the passages had been slipped in by others; the NPNF editors reject that theory. They also warn against claiming Gregory for 'eternal hope' for everyone, since he still speaks of a last judgment. These are Gregory's views, in her voice.
hard_topics.source: On the Soul and the Resurrection (the 'all in all' and 'healed by the Fire' passages); NPNF vol. 5, prolegomena, chapter III 'His Origenism' and the preface: 'nor could Germanus, the Patriarch of Constantinople in the next century, remove it by the device of supposed interpolations'; 'to claim him as one who favours the doctrine of "Eternal Hope" in a universal sense is hardly possible'; 'a canonized saint (for, more fortunate than his works, he was never branded as a heretic)'. NCE: 'the theological views are undoubtedly Gregory's'.
hard_topics.note: Germanus's own text (via Photius, Bibliotheca codex 233) was NOT read; it is reported here only through the NPNF editors. CHECKER 2026-09-25: (1) In the dialogue it is Gregory who sums up ("Then it seems, I said, that it is not punishment chiefly...") and Macrina who agrees ("That, said the Teacher, is my meaning"); the page said she answered his question with no. Fixed. (2) The preface is signed "W. M. July, 1892" (William Moore, a translator), and "His Origenism" is in the translators' prolegomena, so the page now says "the English translators", not "the editors". (3) CCEL pages: preface npnf205.iv.html, Origenism chapter npnf205.vii.iii.html (both opened and the lines found), in place of the 3.5 MB cache/npnf205.txt.

hard_topics.text: She refused to let a doctor examine her, out of modesty, against her mother's plea that medicine is God's gift. Tell it as Gregory tells it, with her mother's words beside it.
hard_topics.source: Life of Macrina, 'They find on the body marks of Macrina's sanctity'

hard_topics.text: She allowed tears only in prayer, and quoted Paul against grieving 'as those without hope'. She held there is only one marriage in a life, even when the betrothed dies before the wedding.
hard_topics.source: Life of Macrina ('One occasion for tears'; 'but one marriage'); On the Soul and the Resurrection, opening
hard_topics.note: Yet she let Gregory weep 'for a little while, like a skilful driver' before reining him in (exact).

hard_topics.text: The family owned slaves. She had her mother live with the maids as equals and sisters. Gregory's Life, in Clarke's translation, does not say they were set free, though the Episcopal Church and the Russian Life say she freed them.
hard_topics.source: Life of Macrina ('treating all her slave girls and menials as if they were sisters'); LFF 2022 ('her decisions to free slaves'); azbyka.ru ('отпустить рабов на свободу')
hard_topics.note: Whether the Greek implies freeing was NOT checked. Do not print either way until checked.

prayer_she_wrote.text: Her dying prayer, as Gregory heard and recorded it. Not written by her hand, but given as her own words. It can be printed whole.
prayer_she_wrote.exact_opening: Thou, O Lord, hast freed us from the fear of death. Thou hast made the end of this life the beginning to us of true life.
prayer_she_wrote.exact_middle: O God eternal, to Whom I have been attached from my mother's womb, Whom my soul has loved with all its strength, to Whom I have dedicated both my flesh and my soul from my youth up until now
prayer_she_wrote.source: Life of Macrina, the part headed 'Macrina's dying prayer' (PG 46.984C-986A)
prayer_she_wrote.note: The full prayer is in sources/.../life-of-macrina-clarke-1916.reading.txt, line 129, capitals already as printed (Thou, Thy, Thee, Whom, Who). One slip in the transcription: 'the gates of .hell' has a stray full stop; check the scan (clarke-1916-archive-ocr.txt) before printing that line.

band.title: Saint Macrina (statue 21 on the north colonnade of St Peter's Square)
band.artist: Unknown sculptor (Bernini's colonnade workshop); photograph by Alf van Beem, 2012
band.licence: CC0 (the photograph, tagged {{CC-zero}}, own work by Alf van Beem). The statue itself is 17th century, public domain.
band.size: 1350 x 1800 px, 267 KB (from the 1830 x 2440 original)
band.alt: A white stone statue of a young woman in a flowing cloak against a deep blue sky; she looks upward, one hand on her breast and a book held in the other.
band.crop: Face at about 50% across, 8 to 12% down: posM '50% 8%', posD '50% 8%' (to be checked at 320 to 390).
band.note: Statue facts from stpetersbasilica.info (an independent site citing Martinelli, 'Le Statue Berniniane del Colonnato di San Pietro', 1987): 'Statue created - 1668', 'Sculptor - unknown', travertine, 3.1 m, 'The young saint dressed in tunic and cloak looks to the sky. The right hand is on her chest and the left is holding a book.' It is a statue, not a painting: no public-domain painting of her with a clear face at 1200 px or more was found. Credit line: 'Saint Macrina, statue on the colonnade of St Peter's Square, 1668. Photo by Alf van Beem, CC0.'

second.title: St Macrina the Younger, fresco in St Sophia Cathedral, Kyiv
second.size: 320 x 768 px, 64 KB (the largest copy on Commons; not enlarged)
second.alt: A fresco of Macrina standing in a grey-green veil and cloak over a white robe, a gold halo behind her head, both hands raised with the palms facing out.
second.note: This is the picture the site already uses (site/public/img/early-christians/macrina-the-younger.jpg). It is small. Commons source: kara-kotsya.narod.ru. The identification as Macrina rests on the Commons description (Russian: 'Преподобная Макрина (фреска Софийского собора в Киеве)'); not checked against the cathedral museum.

personality_test.text: The Christian Personality Test does not name her as a kindred saint of any type, or in any opposite pair. She appears once, in The Herald's card for 'St Basil the Great, as a young man': 'His brother says Basil came home from university proud of his speaking. He looked down on the leading men of his town, until his sister Macrina turned him round.' (src: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina)
personality_test.source: site/src/data/personality.json, TYPES.herald.kindred[2]; OPPOSITES has no Macrina
personality_test.note: The Herald text checks out: 'looked down on the local dignitaries' (Life). So no 'Her personality type' row for her. The hearth research once proposed her for The Hearth ('in every way she tried to be cheerful...'); it was not used.

groups.note: 'cappadocians': she is not one of the three Cappadocian Fathers, but the search brief puts her on the Cappadocian group page ('All three plus Macrina'), and she lived there. 'women': yes. 'monks' (the filter label is 'Monks and hermits'): she led a community of women ascetics and Gregory calls her the abbess; LFF calls her 'Monastic'. Consider relabelling the filter 'Monks, nuns and hermits' so she fits it plainly. Not 'fathers' (not a Church Father; wrote nothing). Not 'teachers' (though the Church of England calls her a 'Teacher of the Faith', the collection is about writers).

side.text: east: correct (Cappadocia and Pontus; her cult reached the West late, NCE).

site_data_flags.text: people.macrina.dates says 'c. 327 to 379'. The best sources say about 330 (Catholic Encyclopedia 1910; NCE), and she died in 379 or 380 (NCE, OCA). Suggest 'About 330 to 379 or 380' (or 'c. 330 to 379' if space is short).
site_data_flags.note: 327 comes only from a weak source; Wikidata offers 324, 327 and 330.

site_data_flags.text: people.macrina.where says 'Cappadocia'. Her adult life was spent in Pontus, at Annesi on the river Iris. Suggest 'Pontus, in today's Turkey' or 'Cappadocia and Pontus'.
cells.calm ends the line with a full stop where the source has a comma, and the passage is about the soul freed from passions 'whether by forethought here, or by purgation hereafter'.
site_data_flags.note: Fair use of the line, but say it is cut short.

site_data_flags.text: cells.deeper begins with a capital 'It' where the source has 'and so it is impossible'; the passage is about one parable (the rich man and Lazarus), not Bible stories in general.

cells.tears and cells.all: CCEL's 1893 text prints inner quotation marks ("grieved for them that sleep", "men without hope"; "all", "in all"); the site's lines match New Advent, which drops them. Both are the same translation.

The research file (group-06.json) quotes 'Why, what is the special pain'; CCEL has 'especial'. It also calls the naucratius death a 'hunting accident', which the Life does not say (Clarke's introduction does).

could_not_verify: How to say her name in a dictionary: no entry in Merriam-Webster, Dictionary.com, Wiktionary or the Century Cyclopedia of Names; Collins returned 403. 'mah-KREE-nuh' is from name sites only. Leave the 'Pronounced' row out until checked.
The Greek original of her dying prayer (PG 46.984C) and of the 'insensible to the divine blessings' rebuke: no free, reliable Greek text was found. Print English only.
Her exact birth year (327, 330 and 340 all appear) and her death year (379 or 380). No ancient source gives either; 19 July as her death day comes from church calendars, not from the Life.
Whether she freed the household's slaves: LFF 2022 and azbyka.ru say so; Clarke's English of the Life says only that she treated them as sisters and equals. The Greek was not checked.

The current (2004) Roman Martyrology's entry for 19 July. Only the 1916 English edition (scan) and a blog transcription of the 1956 Latin edition were read. The 1916 scan prints 'Marcina'; the page image was not viewed to tell a misprint from a scan error.
GOARCH's calendar page (403). The Greek date of 19 July is confirmed from saint.gr instead; the OCA and azbyka.ru agree.
USCCB (403): that 19 July has no memorial of her on the General Roman Calendar was checked on Wikipedia's list of the General Roman Calendar only.
The ELCA date (14 June) is from the final draft of Evangelical Lutheran Worship (2006), not the printed book; and no source says why the ELCA groups her there.
That Basil's letters never name her: checked in the 354 letters of NPNF vol. 8 (English); not checked against the full Greek corpus (about 366 letters).
Gregory of Nyssa's Letter 19 (to John), which describes Macrina as a teacher and a mother to the family: no public-domain English translation found; not quoted.
Germanus of Constantinople's interpolation claim, known through Photius's Bibliotheca, codex 233: read only as reported by the NPNF editors.
The sculptor of the colonnade statue (unknown per stpetersbasilica.info citing Martinelli 1987) and the Kyiv fresco's identification as Macrina (Commons description only).
The exact modern site of Annesi on the Iris.
Patronages: none found; the row should be left out.

fixes: Who: "everything we know comes from him" -> "almost everything" (Basil's Letter 223 and the church calendars are other witnesses; the page's own lede already says almost). "talked Basil out of his pride" -> "turned Basil from his pride" (the Life says she "took him in hand", not that she talked).

The abandoned children: "babies left by the roadside to die" -> "children abandoned by the roadside" (Life: "whom she picked up, exposed by the roadside in the time of famine. She had nursed and reared them"; it does not say babies).
Eye healing: "the skin round one of her eyes" -> "the membrane round her eye" (Life: "the membrane round the eye being enlarged and whitish").

Her last evening: "Toward sunset her couch was turned to the East... prayed aloud in a low voice" -> the couch "had been turned" already (pluperfect in the Life) and she was "whispering with a low voice, so that we could just hear"; "aloud" removed.
Funeral: "the mile" -> "the short way ..., about a mile" (seven or eight stades, about 1.3 to 1.5 km).

Healing fire: Gregory sums up and she agrees (see hard_topics note). The "all in all" item's place was cited as "near the end"; the quoted line sits about two-thirds of the way in, now cited by topic.

Critics: "The editors of the English translation" -> "The English translators" (preface signed W. M.; Origenism chapter in the translators' prolegomena). Sources now link the CCEL preface and chapter pages.
NPNF 8 prolegomena link was the Genealogical Tables page; now npnf208.vi.i.i.html.
In art: dropped "No fixed symbol" (unsourced absence) and "In the East" (one fresco); names the Kyiv fresco instead.

Dialogue quote "Why, what is the especial pain...": context was "her first answer to his grief"; her first response is the Apostle's words, this line answers his objection that everyone dreads death. Reworded.
Macrina the Elder's 14 January is the Roman Martyrology's date (and the NCE's); the page now says so, since the page prints several calendars.
Anglican row note now says the Church of England keeps her as a Lesser Festival (Common Worship, roman type).
Circle: Emmelia's name is not in the Life; cite now adds Clarke's introduction ("His parents, Basil and Emmelia"). Gregory's entry split into two sentences.
Numbers: the "Years apart" source now names the Life's part ("Gregory resolves to visit his sister").
open: The page runs about 4,000 words, well over the 1,000 to 1,800 guide (the whole dying prayer alone is about 380). Every part stands on a checked source; whether to trim is the owner's call.
The Kyiv fresco's identification as Macrina rests on the Commons description only (and it is 320 x 768 px, the largest copy found).
